hints: Start by thinking about which nuclei in the body are useful for imaging and why they behave like tiny magnets.
Consider what happens to those tiny magnets when the patient is placed inside a very strong and uniform magnetic field.
Recall the name and nature of the motion of the nuclei about the field direction and what determines its frequency.
Think about what type of electromagnetic pulse must be applied to interact with the precessing nuclei and the condition for resonance.
Focus on what resonance does to the energy state of the nuclei - what is meant by excitation.
Consider what happens when the applied pulse is switched off and the nuclei return to their original state.
Think about how the signal given out on relaxation can be used to form an image of different tissues.
Finally, think about why a second non-uniform field is needed on top of the uniform field to locate where in the body the signal comes from.
walkthrough:
**Set Up With a Strong Uniform Field**
You and I know the body contains a lot of hydrogen in water and tissue. Each hydrogen proton has spin and a magnetic moment, so it acts like a tiny bar magnet. When the patient goes inside the scanner, they experience a strong uniform magnetic field, typically about $1-3 \text{ T}$. This aligns the moments and makes them precess - that is, rotate - about the direction of the field, just like a spinning top wobbles around the vertical.

**Drive Resonance With an RF Pulse**
The precession happens at one specific frequency called the Larmor frequency, which is proportional to the magnetic field strength. Now a pulse of radio-frequency (RF) radiation is applied. If the RF is at exactly the Larmor frequency, resonance occurs and the nuclei absorb energy. We call this excitation - the nuclei are tipped into a higher energy state and precess in phase.

**Detect Emission on Relaxation**
When the RF pulse is switched off, the excited nuclei relax back to their original alignment. As they de-excite they emit their own RF pulse. Coils around the patient detect this emitted RF signal. Its strength depends on the number of hydrogen nuclei present, so different tissues like fat, muscle, grey matter and tumours give different signal strengths. A computer processes these signals to build up contrast.

**Locate the Signal With a Gradient Field**
A uniform field alone tells us resonance is happening but not where. So a non-uniform gradient field is superposed on the uniform field. This makes the total field strength, and therefore the Larmor frequency, slightly different at each position in the body. Only nuclei in a particular slice or region will be resonant with a given RF frequency. By varying the gradient and the RF frequency, the position of detection can be scanned through the body to build a 3D map of internal structures.

Final answer: Patient is placed in a strong uniform magnetic field. Hydrogen nuclei precess about the field direction at the Larmor frequency. An RF pulse at the Larmor frequency is applied to cause resonance and excitation of the nuclei. On relaxation/de-excitation the nuclei emit RF radiation which is detected and processed to form an image. A non-uniform gradient field is superposed on the uniform field so that the Larmor frequency varies with position, allowing the position of resonating nuclei to be determined.
